overview.content: Groups buttons into one strip, and sets their appearance, size, shape, status and disabled state as a group.

By default only one toggle in a group is pressed at a time, as in a radio group, and clicking it again keeps it
pressed. With `multiple` on the group any number of toggles stays pressed.

The group's value is the value of the pressed toggle, given to a toggle with its `value` input, or `null` when none
is pressed; with `multiple`, it's the values of all pressed toggles, as a select's. Listen to `(valueChange)`, bind
`value` both ways, e.g. `<nb-button-group [(value)]="track">`, to press toggles from the app too, or use the group
in a form, as a radio group, with `formControl`, `ngModel` or `formField`; the values have the type of what it's
bound to.
`disabled` on the group, or its form control, disables all its buttons.

The group's `appearance`, `status`, `size` and `shape` replace those of its buttons.

overview.content: Opens a menu of items from an element, e.g. a profile button, in an overlay beside it.

`nbContextMenuPlacement` puts the menu at the host's `bottom` (default), `top`, `start`, `end`, `left` or `right`,
or at a corner such as `bottom-start`:

```html
<button [nbContextMenu]="items" nbContextMenuPlacement="right"></button>
```

```ts
items = [{ title: 'Profile' }, { title: 'Log out' }];
```

When the menu doesn't fit the viewport it moves to another side, `clockwise` by default; `nbContextMenuAdjustment`
changes that to `counterclockwise`, `vertical`, `horizontal`, or `noop` to keep it where it is:

```html
<button [nbContextMenu]="items" nbContextMenuAdjustment="counterclockwise"></button>
```

```ts
items = [{ title: 'Profile' }, { title: 'Log out' }];
```
`nbContextMenuTrigger` sets what opens and closes the menu:

- `click` (default) opens it with a click on the host and closes it with a click elsewhere on the page. The host
is a disclosure then, with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`; a menu opened by keyboard takes the focus to its
first item, and Escape brings it back.
- `hint` opens it while the pointer is over the host.
- `hover` is `hint`, but the menu stays open while the pointer moves from the host onto it, so its items can be
clicked.
- `focus` opens it while the host has focus.
- `noop` leaves it to `show()`, `hide()` and `toggle()`.

overview.content:
A form control that picks a date, a range or a date with a time in a calendar, which opens under the input when it
is focused or clicked. The input's text is the value in the picker's `format`, and dates typed into it are read
back.

```html
<input [nbDatepicker]="datepicker">
<nb-datepicker #datepicker></nb-datepicker>
```

The input binds to a form control or `ngModel`. The value has the type of the configured `NbDateService`: `Date`
with the native and date-fns services, `Moment` with the moment service. Rangepickers use `NbCalendarRange` with
that type.

The datepicker's `min`, `max` and `filter` limit the dates the calendar offers, and the date typed in the input:
outside them the field has the `nbDatepickerMin`, `nbDatepickerMax` or `nbDatepickerFilter` error. While the text
isn't a date, the value stays the last date and the field has the `nbDatepickerParse` error. The errors are
`{ kind, message, …data }`, with the messages of `nb-validation-errors`, in reactive, template-driven and signal
forms alike.
`filter` is a predicate that receives a date and returns whether it can be picked.

`pickerMode="month"` or `"year"` picks a month or a year, e.g. a card's expiry or a graduation year: the calendar
starts on the months or the years, and the value is the first day of the one picked. Its text is in the date
service's month or year format (`2026-03`, `2026`), or the datepicker's `format`, e.g. `MMM yyyy` with date-fns.

`nb-date-timepicker` picks a time along with the date; the value is applied with its OK button:

```html
<input nbInput placeholder="Pick Date" [nbDatepicker]="dateTimePicker">
<nb-date-timepicker withSeconds #dateTimePicker></nb-date-timepicker>
```
With `singleColumn` the times are one list, `step` minutes apart, instead of hour and minute columns:

The dialog closes with a result, `dialogRef.close(result)`, which the opener gets from `onClose`:

### Configuration

`open` takes options, and `provideNbDialog` or `NbDialogModule.forRoot({ ... })` sets their defaults:

`context` - data for the content: a component gets it as its inputs, a template as `$implicit`.

```ts
this.dialogService.open(template, { context: 'pass data in template' });
```

```html

```

`hasBackdrop` - shows a backdrop under the dialog, which makes it modal. Default is true.
`closeOnBackdropClick` - closes the dialog with a click on the backdrop. Default is true.
`closeOnEsc` - closes the dialog with Escape. Default is true.

`closeOnNavigation` - closes the dialog on router navigation, e.g. when the browser's back button is pressed.
Default is true.

`hasScroll` - lets the page scroll under the dialog. Default is false: the page can't scroll while a dialog is
open. Open the dialogs in a separate window and try to scroll.

`autoFocus` - focuses the dialog's first focusable element once it opens, or at least takes the focus off the
element that opened it, and returns the focus when it closes. Default is true. Without it the focus stays on the
opener, so Space opens the same dialog again: open the dialogs in a separate window, click the button without
focus and press Space a few times.

`position` - where the dialog appears: `center` (default), `top`, `bottom`, or a corner such as `bottom-start` or
`top-right`, with `positionOffset` as the space to the viewport edges. A dialog without a backdrop in a corner
suits notices such as a cookie consent.

### Confirm dialog

`confirm` asks the user to confirm an action and resolves to whether they did. Pass `action` to run it from the
dialog: it stays open while the action runs, so a failed request can be retried, and closes once it succeeds.
Set the default button texts and status, e.g. to translate them, with `provideNbConfirmDialog`.

overview.content: Renders an SVG or font icon from a registered icon pack.
Uses the icons of `@liquid-js/lyr-icons` by default, once they're registered.

```html
<nb-icon icon="star"></nb-icon>
```
### Installation

Import `NbIconComponent` into your standalone component:
```ts
@Component({
  imports: [NbIconComponent],
})
export class PageComponent { }
```

By default Lyra comes only with the icons its components use. The rest of its icons ship as a separate package,
`@liquid-js/lyr-icons`:
```sh
npm i @liquid-js/lyr-icons
```
Register it in the application's providers, which makes it the default pack:
```ts
import { provideNbIcons } from '@liquid-js/lyr-icons';

bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, { providers: [provideNbTheme(), provideNbIcons()] });
```
All the icons are in the [icon browser](icons/browse-icons); an app's own icons can join the pack, see
[Register Icon Packs](icons/register-icon-packs).

### Usage

`status` colours the icon:
```html
<nb-icon icon="star" status="warning"></nb-icon>
```

`pack` takes the icon from a pack other than the default one:
```html
<nb-icon icon="star" pack="font-awesome"></nb-icon>
```
`options` passes settings the icon pack supports, if any:

```html
<nb-icon icon="star" [options]="{ animation: { type: 'zoom' } }"></nb-icon>
```

The icons animate with `zoom`, `pulse`, `shake` or `flip`; `infinite: true` repeats it, and `hover: false` plays it
right away instead of on hover:

```html
<nb-icon icon="heart-outline" [options]="{ animation: { type: 'pulse', infinite: true, hover: false } }"></nb-icon>
```

Options in a `nb-select` that open from a row, as a tree. Only the options in them are selected, not the nested
options themselves. Nested options can hold more nested options, and sit in groups.

```html

  <nb-option value="local">This device</nb-option>
  <nb-option-nested title="Cloud">
    <nb-option value="drive">Google Drive</nb-option>
    <nb-option-nested title="Object storage">
      <nb-option value="s3">AWS S3</nb-option>
    </nb-option-nested>
  </nb-option-nested>
</nb-select>
```

A row opens and closes on click, Enter or Space; ArrowRight opens it, or moves into it when it's open, and ArrowLeft
closes it or moves to its parent. The list shows up to `nestedLevels` levels of the select at once (3 by default):
opening a deeper one drills in, so the list starts at a nested option, with a row to go back. A collapsed row shows
when an option in it is selected, and opens to show an option that becomes active, e.g. the selected one as the
list opens. A search shows the matching options with the nested options they're in.

can be used.
- `focus` shows it while the focus is in the host or the popover, and hides it on a click outside both.
- `noop` leaves it to `show()`, `hide()` and `toggle()`.

overview.content: A dropdown that selects one of its `nb-option`s, or several with `multiple`.

With `chips`, a multiple select shows its selected options as tags. The select keeps its background under the
pointer while it shows them, as a tag list with an input does, so the tags stay apart from the field:

With `searchable`, the open list has a search input that filters the options by their text, ignoring case and
accents; `searchFn` changes how options match. Focus stays in the input, and the arrow keys, Home, End and Enter
work the list:

In a multiple select, `<nb-option selectAll>` selects all enabled options (the ones a search shows), or clears them
when they're all selected; its checkbox shows when only some are. `maxSelections` caps how many options the user can
select, disabling the rest until one is deselected:

Long lists stay fast: with 100 or more options shown, the list lays out only the ones near its view, and the rest
keep their place in the scroll. Options are still written as usual, e.g. with `@for`, can differ in height, and work
with search, the keyboard and assistive technology; this applies to every list of `nb-option`s, including
autocomplete.

An option without a value clears the selection, as writing `null` or `undefined` does.

With `nullable`, `null` is a value like any other: an option with a `null` value, e.g. "Auto", is selected and shown
when the value is `null`, and only options without a value clear the selection.
The `ghost` appearance shows no background or border until the select is hovered, focused or open:

overview.content: A sidebar of the layout, e.g. for a menu, that expands, compacts or collapses.

A `responsive` sidebar follows the screen size: it compacts on the `compactedBreakpoints`, collapses on the
`collapsedBreakpoints`, and expands again on the larger ones.

With a `subheader` header, the header sits beside the sidebar rather than above it:
```html
<nb-layout-header subheader></nb-layout-header>
```

The sidebar then has no shadow, and the header can't be `fixed`.

A sidebar that overlays the content, as a `fixed` or a responsive one does on smaller screens, can close itself
when it's expanded: `closeOnNavigation` closes it when the router navigates or a link in it is picked, and
`closeOnOutsideClick` when the user clicks outside it. It then compacts on tablets and collapses otherwise. A
click that expands the sidebar, e.g. on a toggle button in the header, doesn't close it.

overview.content:
Shows an element as a placeholder while its content loads: the content is hidden and the element's own box is
painted, with a shimmer whose waves move across the page at a steady pace, over all placeholders as one.

```html

{{ user?.name ?? 'Jane Doe' }}

```

The placeholder takes the shape of the content, so give it sample content while loading, e.g. a typical name. On an
inline element, such as a `span` in a paragraph, each line of text is its own bar. `nbSkeletonShape="circle"`
rounds it, e.g. for an avatar, and `nbSkeletonWidth` sizes an element with no content yet.

While loading, the element is `inert`: its sample content can't be focused or clicked, and assistive technologies
skip it. Tell them the region is loading on the region itself, e.g. with `aria-busy="true"`. The shimmer stands
still when the user prefers reduced motion.

overview.content: A slider picks a number, or a range with `range`, by dragging a thumb along a track, or with the keyboard.

```html
<nb-slider [min]="0" [max]="100" [step]="5" formControlName="volume" />
<nb-slider range [min]="0" [max]="500" formControlName="price" />
```

A range's value is `{ start, end }`; its thumbs can pass each other, and swap. `step` snaps values to steps from
`min`, and `ticks` marks them on the track (or every n-th one, `[ticks]="5"`). `min`, `max` and the `center` show
as labels under the track, and the value shows above the thumb while it moves or has the keyboard focus;
`formatValue` formats both.

Leave out `min` or `max` and that end is open: the track reaches a little past the values on it, so moving a thumb
towards the open end takes the end along, and any value can be reached while small values get most of the track,
e.g. a licence for any number of seats from 1. `center` is where the fill starts and the value without one, e.g. 0
for an adjustment either way.

It comes in the controls' sizes, `tiny` to `giant`, which scale its thumb and track, and takes the app's size for
controls, or its own `slider` default, as the other controls do; its status is `primary` by default, as a checked
checkbox shows.

`transform` draws the track's positions differently: `sqrt` and `log` give the low end more room, e.g. for prices
or file sizes, or give it any increasing function on 0..1. The pointer picks the step it has reached. A value given
to the slider outside `min` or `max` opens that end, so it shows where it is, along with its error.

`vertical` stands the slider up; it's as tall as `slider-vertical-height`, or its own height.

Arrow keys move a thumb a step (or a hundredth of the track without one), Page Up and Page Down ten, and Home and
End to the limits, or ten steps on an open end. A thumb is a `slider`; a range's thumbs are named "Start" and
"End" after the slider's label, e.g. from `nbLabel` or `aria-label`. A value outside `min` and `max` has the `min`
or `max` error, and a range whose start is after its end `nbSliderOrder`.

overview.content:
Steps through a process one `nb-step` at a time: numbered labels in a header, with the selected step's content
under them.

### Installation Import `NbStepperComponent`, `NbStepComponent` into your standalone component: ```ts @Component({ imports: [NbStepperComponent, NbStepComponent], }) export class PageComponent { } ``` With NgModules: Import `NbStepperModule` to your feature module. ```ts @NgModule({ imports: [ // ... NbStepperModule, ], }) export class PageModule { } ``` ### Usage A step's `label` is text, or a template for anything else: ```html ...
Step two
 ... ``` The stepper is `linear` by default: a step can be reached only once the steps before it are completed, so the user can go back, but forward only one step at a time. A step is completed once the user has left it, or when it's marked `completed`; `linear="false"` lets the user pick any step.

With a form as a step's `stepControl`, the step is completed only while the form is valid, so a linear stepper
moves on only when it is:
```html
<nb-stepper orientation="horizontal">
  <nb-step label="Step one" [stepControl]="form">
    <form [formGroup]="form">
      ...
    </form>
  </nb-step>
  ...
</nb-stepper>
```
The steps run across (`horizontal`, the default) or down (`vertical`):

The steps in the header are buttons: a click, Enter or Space selects one. `disableStepNavigation` turns that off,
so the user moves only with `nbStepperPrevious` and `nbStepperNext` buttons.

background under the pointer, and a filled basic tag in it darkens under the pointer rather than lightening, so
the tags never match the field:

```ts
provideNbTheme({
  name: 'default',
  themes: [
    { name: 'default', scheme: 'light' },
    { name: 'dark', scheme: 'dark' },
  ],
  preferences: true,
})
```

```html
<nb-theme-select />
```

It offers the themes the app declares in `provideNbTheme`, named with their `label`, and "System": the declared
theme that fits the system's colour scheme and contrast, which it follows as they change, and which is the theme
until the user picks one. A high-contrast theme (`contrast: 'more'`) is picked when the system asks for more
contrast. With `preferences`, the choice is kept in `NB_PREFERENCE_STORAGE`, `localStorage` by default; provide

```ts
{
  provide: NB_PREFERENCE_STORAGE,
  useValue: { get: (key) => profile.get(key), set: (key, value) => profile.set(key, value) },
}
```

overview.content:
A form control on an input that picks a time: the time picker opens when the input gets focus, and the input's
text is parsed as the user types.

Arrow Down in the input moves into the timepicker, a named dialog, to its selected time. Its columns are listboxes:
the arrow keys, Home, End, Page Up and Page Down move in a column, Enter or Space picks, and Tab goes to the next
column. Escape closes it, keeping the time, back in the input.
```html
<input [nbTimepicker]="timepicker">
<nb-timepicker #timepicker></nb-timepicker>
```

`twelveHoursFormat` on the time picker forces 12-hour times; by default it follows the `provideNbTimepicker()`
config, or else the application's locale.

```html
<input [nbTimepicker]="timepicker">
<nb-timepicker #timepicker twelveHoursFormat></nb-timepicker>
```

`singleColumn` lists whole times instead of hours and minutes to pick separately; `step` sets the minutes between
them, e.g. 11:00, 11:20, 11:40…
The input is a form control, so `formControl` and `ngModel` go on it:

```html
<input [nbTimepicker]="timepicker" [formControl]="formControl">
<nb-timepicker #timepicker></nb-timepicker>
```

```html
<input [nbTimepicker]="timepicker" [ngModel]="date">
<nb-timepicker #timepicker></nb-timepicker>
```

### Validation

`min` and `max` on the timepicker limit the times to pick, by time of day: the list disables the others. Text in
the input that isn't a time has the `nbTimepickerParse` error, and the value stays the last time, as Angular's
controls report text they can't parse; a time out of range has `nbTimepickerMin` or `nbTimepickerMax`, with
`minText` or `maxText`. Emptying the input clears the value. Errors are `{ kind, message, …data }`, and
`nb-validation-errors` shows them:

```html
<input nbInput [nbTimepicker]="picker" formControlName="start" nbValidation #start="nbValidation" />
<nb-timepicker #picker [min]="opens" [max]="closes" />
<nb-validation-errors [for]="start" />
```

The texts come from `NbTextsService`'s `timepicker` texts. The config's `localization`, passed to
`provideNbTimepicker()` or `NbTimepickerModule.forRoot()`, overrides them:
```ts
provideNbTimepicker({
  localization: {
    hoursText: 'Hr',
    minutesText: 'Min',
    secondsText: 'Sec',
    ampmText: 'Am/Pm',
  },
})
```

`nbLabel` labels the field, and marks it while it's required, see `NbLabelComponent`:

```html
<label nbLabel [for]="password">Password</label>
```

Its content is the field's helper text, which shows while the field shows no errors and gives way to them; it
describes the field too, and can have markup such as links. Errors and the helper text open and close smoothly as
they change, whatever their content and length, unless the user prefers reduced motion:

kind, the message a signal forms rule gave, the messages set with `provideNbValidation`, the texts set with
`provideNbTexts({ validation })`, and the message the error's value carries, e.g.

own controls; provide your own to translate them or to add messages for custom validators. Lyra's controls put the
same message in their errors' values, `{ kind, message, …data }`.

`status()`.

`provideNbValidation({ trigger })` to show them sooner (`dirty`) or later (`submitted`).

```html
<nb-color-picker [formControl]="color" [presets]="['#3366ff', '#00d68f']" clearable />
```

### Installation

Install [`nxt-color-picker`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/nxt-color-picker), which draws the dialog, and import
`NbColorPickerComponent` from `@liquid-js/lyr-extras/color-picker`:

```bash
npm install nxt-color-picker
```

### Usage

It's a form control whose value is the colour as text, e.g. `#3366ff`, or `null` without one. The user picks it in
the dialog or types it, and with `clearable` the field has a button that clears it, as does emptying the text. It
has the sizes, statuses, shapes and `ghost` look of `nbInput`, and its `readonly`, without the dialog; its swatch
shows the colour over a checkerboard, so transparency shows:

The dialog opens below the field when it has focus, as the date picker's does, and closes when focus or a click
goes elsewhere. Arrow Down moves focus into it, where the sliders move with the arrow keys, Page Up and Down, Home
and End; Enter and Escape close it, keeping the colour, and return to the field.

`outputFormat` picks the text the value has, `hex`, `rgba`, `hsla` or `auto`, `alphaChannel` whether it can be
transparent, and `cmyk` adds a CMYK input and makes the value a `cmyk()` colour. The dialog has the theme's
colours, with its own `color-picker-*` variables, which follow the date picker's values.

### Validation

While the text isn't a colour, e.g. `#12345`, the value stays the last colour, and the field has the
`nbColorPicker` parse error, `{ kind, message }`, as Angular's controls report text they can't parse; so does
empty text in a field that isn't `clearable`. It works with `formControl`, `formControlName`, `ngModel` and signal
forms' `[formField]`, and with `nbValidation`:

### Texts

Its texts, and the dialog's, are in the `colorPicker` section of Lyra's texts:

```ts
provideNbTexts({ colorPicker: { clear: 'Remove the color', ok: 'Apply' } })
```

overview.content: A markdown editor, with a toolbar, a preview and a WYSIWYG mode:

```html
<nb-markdown-editor [formControl]="text" aria-label="Description" />
```

### Installation

Install [`@liquid-js/underflow`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@liquid-js/underflow), which is the editor, with the
ProseMirror and DOMPurify packages it uses, and import `NbMarkdownEditorComponent` from
`@liquid-js/lyr-extras/markdown-editor`:

```bash
npm install @liquid-js/underflow prosemirror-commands prosemirror-history prosemirror-inputrules \
  prosemirror-keymap prosemirror-model prosemirror-state prosemirror-transform prosemirror-view dompurify
```

The Format button formats with [`remark`](https://remark.js.org), which it loads when it's first used, with
`remark-gfm` and `remark-frontmatter`:

```bash
npm install remark remark-gfm remark-frontmatter
```

The editor loads when the first one shows; its styles come with the component. It highlights code with the
highlight.js that [`nxt-highlightjs`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/nxt-highlightjs) loads, when the app sets it up
as in `nb-markdown-viewer`, so install them too:

```bash
npm install nxt-highlightjs highlight.js
```

### Usage

It's a form control whose value is the markdown, CommonMark with GitHub's extensions, e.g. tables and task lists.
Its frame has the colours of a field and its `status`, and the text the theme's styles:

The preview shows the text's straight quotes, `--`, `---` and `...` as typographic quotes, en and em dashes and
ellipses, as `nb-markdown-viewer` does, while the markdown and the WYSIWYG mode keep them as written.

In the markdown mode the preview is a tab, or next to the markdown with `previewStyle="vertical"`; the WYSIWYG mode
edits the formatted text, and `mode` is the one that shows. The toolbar wraps onto more lines when it doesn't fit,
so all of its buttons can be reached with Tab; `toolbarItems` picks them.

The Format button, and Shift+Alt+F in the text, writes the markdown in one style with `nbFormatMarkdown`, which
also writes typographic quotes, dashes and ellipses as plain characters; Undo brings the text back. It's `format` in
`toolbarItems`.

In the text, Tab indents list items and moves between table cells, so Escape and then Tab or Shift+Tab moves focus
out of it, as in code editors. Name the text with `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby` for a `label`, or an `nbLabel` with
`nbValidation`, which also gives it the field's status and errors, as it does an input.

With `readonly` the text can be read, selected and copied, but not changed, as in a read-only field: the toolbar
and the mode switch are disabled, while the Write and Preview tabs still switch. Disabled, the editor is read-only
too, in the colours of a disabled field, and Tab skips it.

Text that mixes right-to-left and left-to-right languages, e.g. Arabic or Hebrew quoted in English, reads right
with `autoDirection`: each paragraph, heading, list, quote and table takes the direction of its own text, as
`dir="auto"` does, in the preview and the WYSIWYG mode, and so does each line of the markdown. Code blocks read left
to right. The markdown itself doesn't change.

`options` takes the [editor's other options](https://liquid-js.github.io/underflow/docs/), e.g. plugins, widgets
or `hooks.addImageBlobHook` to upload pasted images, and `editor()` is the editor, for its methods. It's made again
when the options, the toolbar, the texts or `autoDirection` change, keeping the markdown.


### Installation It renders the markdown with Angular's templates through [`ngx-remark`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/ngx-remark), which parses it with [`remark`](https://remark.js.org), [`remark-gfm`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/remark-gfm) and [`remark-smartypants`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/remark-smartypants), and highlights code with [`nxt-highlightjs`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/nxt-highlightjs); install them and import `NbMarkdownViewerComponent` from `@liquid-js/lyr-extras/markdown-viewer`. ```sh npm install ngx-remark remark remark-gfm remark-smartypants nxt-highlightjs highlight.js ``` `remark` uses a CommonJS module, `extend`, which Angular's build warns about unless it's in `allowedCommonJsDependencies` in `angular.json`. ### Usage The markdown is CommonMark with GitHub's extensions: tables, task lists, strikethrough, autolinks and footnotes. It renders as the editor's preview shows it, on the server too, so a prerendered page has the text before scripts run. The text's straight quotes, `--`, `---` and `...` show as typographic quotes, en and em dashes and ellipses, so the markdown can keep the plain characters that the editor's Format button writes; code shows them as they are. overview.content: Formats what the user types in a field with a mask, e.g. a phone number or a card number:

```html
<input nbInput type="tel" [nbMask]="'(###) ###-####'" formControlName="phone" />
```

### Installation

It formats with [`maska`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/maska); install it and import `NbMaskDirective` from
`@liquid-js/lyr-extras/mask`.

```sh
npm install maska
```

### Usage

In the mask, `#` is a digit, `@` a letter and `*` either; other characters are shown as they are. A list of masks
picks the one that fits the length of what's typed, e.g. `['#### ####', '#### #### ####']`, and a function gives
the mask for what's typed. `nbMaskOptions` takes maska's other options, e.g. `eager` to show the mask's next
characters before they're typed, `tokens` of your own, or `number` for numbers in the app's format.

The form value is what the user typed, without the mask's characters, e.g. `2015550123`, or with
`nbMaskValue="masked"`, the text as shown, `(201) 555-0123`. While the text doesn't fill the mask, the value stays
the last complete one, or empty, and the field has the `nbMask` parse error, `{ kind, message }`, as Angular's
controls report text they can't parse; an empty field passes. It works with `formControl`, `formControlName`,
`ngModel` and signal forms' `[formField]`.
It works on text, search, URL, phone and password inputs.

overview.content: Plays audio in a compact bar with Lyra's controls: play, the position, volume and speed.

```html
<nb-audio src="episode.mp3" aria-label="Episode 12" />
```

Audio files play in the browser. Streams play with an engine from Video.js 10, which `provideNbMediaPlayer` sets for
their kind of source and loads when a player first needs it.

It tells when it plays, pauses and ends, its position as it plays, and when it can't play its source, with the
`play`, `pause`, `ended`, `timeUpdate` and `error` events. Without `controls`, it plays unseen, e.g. a sound that
`togglePlay()` plays.

With the focus on it, the keyboard controls it: space or `k` plays and pauses, the left and right arrows seek, Home
and End go to the start and the end, up and down set the volume and `m` mutes.

### Installation

The player needs `@videojs/core`, `@videojs/media` and `@videojs/store`, under the Apache 2.0 licence, which an app
installs only when it uses it; import `NbAudioComponent` from `@liquid-js/lyr-extras/media`:

```bash
npm install @videojs/core @videojs/media @videojs/store
```

overview.content:
Plays a video with Lyra's controls: play, the position, volume, speed, quality, captions, picture in picture and full
screen, as far as the video and the browser have them.

```html
<nb-video src="lesson.mp4" poster="lesson.jpg"
  [tracks]="[{ src: 'lesson.en.vtt', srclang: 'en', label: 'English' }]" />
```

Video files play in the browser. Streams and embeds play with an engine from Video.js 10, which
`provideNbMediaPlayer` sets for their kind of source and loads when a player first needs it:

```ts
provideNbMediaPlayer(withMediaEngines({ hls: () => import('@videojs/hlsjs-video').then((m) => m.HlsJsAdapter) }))
```

It tells when it plays, pauses and ends, its position as it plays, and when it can't play its source:

```html
<nb-video src="lesson.mp4" (ended)="next()" (timeUpdate)="progress.set($event)" (error)="report($event)" />
```

`startTime` starts each source further in, e.g. where the viewer left off, and `seek(time)` goes to a position, also
before the video has loaded.

Without `controls`, it's just the video, e.g. one playing silently in the background:

```html
<nb-video src="clouds.mp4" [controls]="false" autoplay muted loop />
```

It's 16:9 until its `aspect-ratio` says otherwise. With the focus on it, the keyboard controls it: space or `k`
plays and pauses, the left and right arrows seek, Home and End go to the start and the end, up and down set the
volume, `m` mutes, `c` shows captions and `f` goes full screen.

overview.content: A phone number field with the country's flag, which picks the country:

```html
<nb-phone-input formControlName="phone" />
```

### Installation

It parses and formats numbers with [`libphonenumber-js`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/libphonenumber-js), names
the countries with [`i18n-iso-countries`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/i18n-iso-countries)' language files, and
shows flags with [`nxt-flags`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/nxt-flags); install them and import
`NbPhoneInputComponent` from `@liquid-js/lyr-extras/phone-input`.

```sh
npm install libphonenumber-js i18n-iso-countries nxt-flags
```

The flags are images the app serves from `assets/flags`; add them to the assets in `angular.json`:

```json
{ "glob": "*.svg", "input": "node_modules/nxt-flags/assets/flags", "output": "assets/flags" }
```

To serve them from elsewhere, e.g. a CDN, set the path with `provideFlagsPath()` from `nxt-flags`.

### Usage

The user types the number in their country's format or with a calling code, e.g. `+44`, which picks the country.
The flag button replaces the field with a search of the countries, by name or calling code; Escape goes back.
The country is the one of the app's locale (`LOCALE_ID`) until the user or a number picks another, or set it with
`country`, which also tells which one is picked. It has the sizes, statuses, shapes and `ghost` look of `nbInput`,
and its `placeholder` and `readonly`; the placeholder is an example number of the country by default.

The value is the number in the `E.164` format, e.g. `+12015550123`, or `null` without one; when the field leaves,
it shows the number in its country's format, `(201) 555-0123`. While the text isn't a valid number, the value
stays the last valid one, or `null`, and the field has the `nbPhoneNumber` parse error,
`{ kind, problem: 'invalid', message }`, as Angular's controls report text they can't parse; so validators never
see the text. A number from a country that isn't in `countries`, which the list offers, has the same error with
`problem: 'country'`. The errors work in reactive, template-driven and signal forms alike.

It works with `formControl`, `formControlName`, `ngModel` and signal forms' `[formField]`.

### Validators

Phone numbers in other fields, e.g. a text field or data from elsewhere, are checked the same way with validators:
`nbPhoneNumberValidator(options)` in reactive forms, the `nbPhoneNumber` attribute in template-driven forms, and
`nbPhoneNumber(path, options)` in signal forms. The options are the `country` of numbers without a
calling code, the app locale's by default, and the `countries` whose numbers pass, each a value or a function that
gives it, and the `message` of the errors, a text or a function of what's wrong, in place of the app's. Their
`nbPhoneNumber` error says what's wrong, `invalid` or `country`, with its message.

```ts
readonly phone = new FormControl<string | null>(null, nbPhoneNumberValidator({ countries: ['US', 'CA'] }));

readonly contactForm = form(this.contact, (path) => {
  nbPhoneNumber(path.phone, { countries: ['GB'] });
});
```

```html
<input nbInput type="tel" name="support" ngModel nbPhoneNumber [nbPhoneNumberCountries]="['US', 'CA']" />
```

### Country names

The countries are named in English. For other languages, provide the language file of `i18n-iso-countries`, e.g.
per locale's build, or loaded by `LOCALE_ID`:

```ts
providers: [provideNbCountryNames(() => import('i18n-iso-countries/langs/de.json'))]
```

Countries without a name in the file aren't in the list; their numbers are still accepted.

overview.content: Shows `data` as a QR code, e.g. a link to open on a phone:

```html
<nb-qr-code data="https://liquid-js.github.io/lyra/" />
```

### Installation

Install [`@liquid-js/qr-code-styling`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@liquid-js/qr-code-styling), which draws the
code, and import `NbQrCodeComponent` from `@liquid-js/lyr-extras/qr-code`:

```bash
npm install @liquid-js/qr-code-styling @liquid-js/qrcode-generator
```

The library loads when the first code shows. The code also renders on the server, e.g. when a page is
prerendered, so it's in the page as an SVG before scripts run; the library's Node build draws it there and needs:

```bash
npm install @xmldom/xmldom
```

The server leaves out a logo set by `options.image`, which the browser then adds.

### Usage

The code is 10rem wide and scales with its width. It's dark on white, which phones read most reliably, also in
dark themes: set `color` and `background-color` to change that, keeping a strong contrast.

`options` takes the [library's options](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@liquid-js/qr-code-styling), e.g. the dot
shapes, a logo in the middle or a gradient, over the defaults. `download()` saves the code as an SVG or an
image in the colours it shows with:

It's an image named by `aria-label`, or by its data without one. In the browser it's drawn on a canvas by the
library, aligned to the screen's pixels and scaled down from a larger drawing, so the modules don't show seams
where their edges fall between pixels; it's drawn again when its size or the theme changes.
